questions.problem:
Which of the following pairs $(x,y)$ are solutions of the Diophantine equation $5x+2y=75?$

I. $(11,10)$

II. $(10,15)$

III. $(5,25)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's check each pair in turn.

- $(11,10)$ is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting $x=11$ and $y=10,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2y & =75 \\ 5\cdot 11+2\cdot 10 & =75 \\ 55+20 & =75 \\ 75 & =75\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $(10,15)$ is *not* a solution of our equation. Substituting $x=10$ and $y=15,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2y & =75 \\ 5\cdot 10+2\cdot 15 & =75 \\ 50+30 & =75 \\ 80 & \ne 75\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $(5,25)$ is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting $x=5$ and $y=25,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+2y & =75 \\ 5\cdot 5+2\cdot 25 & =75 \\ 25+50 & =75 \\ 75 & =75\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following Diophantine equations have solutions?

I. $4x+12y=6$

II. $2x+12y=4$

III. $-3x+5y=2$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d\,|\,c,$ where $d=\text{gcd}(a,b).$  

With that in mind, let's examine each equation in turn.

- Equation I has no solution. We have $a=4,$ $b=12,$ and $c=6.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(4,12)=4
$$

and $4\,\text{⧸}|\,6,$ our equation has no solution.

- Equation II has solutions. We have $a=2,$ $b=12,$ and $c=4.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(2,12)=2
$$

and $2\,|\,4,$ our equation has solutions.

- Equation III has solutions. We have $a=-3,$ $b=5,$ and $c=2.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(-3,5)=1
$$

and $1\,|\,2,$ our equation has solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem: Given that $(x,y)=(1,-2)$ is a solution of the Diophantine equation $3x+6y=-9,$ and that $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x,$ what is the value of $\overset{∼}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d\,|\,c,$ where $d=\text{gcd}(a,b).$  Moreover, if $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ is a solution to the equation, then the general solution is given by

$$
({x}_{0}+\frac{b}{d}t,\,{y}_{0}-\frac{a}{d}t),\,t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…
$$

Here, we have $a=3,$ $b=6,$ $c=-9,$ and

$$
d=\text{gcd}(3,6)=3.
$$

Since $(1,-2)$ is a solution of $3x+6y=-9,$ the general solution must be

$$
(1+\frac{6}{3}t,\,-2-\frac{3}{3}t)=(1+2t,\,-2-t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=1+2t$ is attained when $t=0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=1+2\cdot 0=1.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $4x+7y=9.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=4,$ $b=7,$ and $c=9.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(7,4)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7 & = & 4\cdot 1 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 4 & = & 3\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =7-4\cdot 1 \\ 1 & =4-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4-3 \\  & =4-(7-4) \\  & =4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot 2+7\cdot (-1) & =1 \\ 4\cdot 2\cdot 9+7\cdot (-1)\cdot 9 & =9 \\ 4\cdot 18+7\cdot (-9) & =9,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(18,-9)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(18+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-9-\frac{a}{d}t)=(18+7t,\,-9-4t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=18+7t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=18+7\cdot (-2)=4.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $9x+11y=6.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the greatest possible negative value of $y.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{y}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=9,$ $b=11,$ and $c=6.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(9,11)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}11 & = & 9\cdot 1 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 9 & = & 2\cdot 4 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =11-9 \\ 1 & =9-2\cdot 4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =9-2\cdot 4 \\  & =9-4(11-9) \\  & =9\cdot 5+11\cdot (-4).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
9\cdot 5+11\cdot (-4)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $6,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9\cdot 5+11\cdot (-4) & =1 \\ 9\cdot 5\cdot 6+11\cdot (-4)\cdot 6 & =6 \\ 9\cdot 30+11\cdot (-24) & =6,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(30,-24)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(30+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-24-\frac{a}{d}t)=(30+11t,\,-24-9t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The greatest possible negative value of $y=-24-9t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{y}=-24-9\cdot (-2)=-6.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=3,$ $b=11,$ and $c=7.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(3,11)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}11 & = & 3\cdot 3 & + & 2 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 3 & = & 2\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =11-9 \\ 1 & =3-2\cdot 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3-2\cdot 1 \\  & =3-(11-9) \\  & =3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot 4+11\cdot (-1) & =1 \\ 3\cdot 4\cdot 7+11\cdot (-1)\cdot 7 & =7 \\ 3\cdot 28+11\cdot (-7) & =7,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(28,-7)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(28+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-7-\frac{a}{d}t)=(28+11t,\,-7-3t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=28+11t$ is attained when $t=-2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=28+11\cdot (-2)=6.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $5x+6y=9.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=5,$ $b=6,$ and $c=9.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(5,6)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}6 & = & 5\cdot 1 & + & 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 5 & = & 1\cdot 5 & + & 0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =6-5\cdot 1.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
5\cdot (-1)+6=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot (-1)+6 & =1 \\ 5\cdot (-1)\cdot 9+6\cdot 9 & =9 \\ 5\cdot (-9)+6\cdot 9 & =9,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(-9,9)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(-9+\frac{b}{d}t,\,9-\frac{a}{d}t)=(-9+6t,\,9-5t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=-9+6t$ is attained when $t=2.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=-9+6\cdot 2=3.
$$

questions.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $5x+9y=8.$ The integer pair $(\overset{∼}{x},\overset{∼}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x.$ What is the value of $\overset{∼}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=5,$ $b=9,$ and $c=8.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(5,9)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}9 & = & 5\cdot 1 & + & 4 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 5 & = & 4\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =9-5\cdot 1 \\ 1 & =5-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =5-4 \\  & =5-(9-5) \\  & =5\cdot 2+9\cdot (-1).\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b)=1$ and

$$
5\cdot 2+9\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $8,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\cdot 2+9\cdot (-1) & =1 \\ 5\cdot 2\cdot 8+9\cdot (-1)\cdot 8 & =8 \\ 5\cdot 16+9\cdot (-8) & =8,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(16,-8)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
(16+\frac{b}{d}t,\,-8-\frac{a}{d}t)=(16+9t,\,-8-5t),
$$

where $t=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…\,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=16+9t$ is attained when $t=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{∼}{x}=16+9\cdot (-1)=7.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying a Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following pairs $(x,y)$ are solutions of the Diophantine equation $3x+8y=5?$

I. $(7,-2)$

II. $(22,-8)$

III. $(15,-5)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's check each pair in turn.

- $(7,-2)$ is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting $x=7$ and $y=-2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+8y & =5 \\ 3\cdot 7+8\cdot (-2) & =5 \\ 21-16 & =5 \\ 5 & =5\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- $(22,-8)$ is *not* a solution of our equation. Substituting $x=22$ and $y=-8,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+8y & =5 \\ 3\cdot 22+8\cdot (-8) & =5 \\ 66-64 & =5 \\ 2 & \ne 5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- $(15,-5)$ is a solution of our equation. Indeed, substituting $x=15$ and $y=-5,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+8y & =5 \\ 3\cdot 15+8\cdot (-5) & =5 \\ 45-40 & =5 \\ 5 & =5\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Identifying Whether a Linear Diophantine Equation Has a Solution
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following Diophantine equations have solutions?

I. $18x+15y=24$

II. $7x-28y=10$

III. $9x+27y=16$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d \: | \: c,$ where $d = \text{gcd}(a,b).$  

With that in mind, let's examine each equation in turn.

- Equation I has solutions. We have $a=18,$ $b=15,$ and $c=24.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(18,15)=3
$$

and $3 \: | \: 24,$ our equation has solutions.

- Equation II has no solution. We have $a=7,$ $b=-28,$ and $c=10.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(7,-28)=7
$$

and $7 \!\not{|}\: 10,$ our equation has no solution.

- Equation III has no solution. We have $a=9,$ $b=27,$ and $c=16.$ Since

$$
d=\text{gcd}(9,27)=9
$$

and $9 \!\not{|}\: 16,$ our equation has no solution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the General Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation Given One of Its Solutions
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $(x,y)=(15,14)$ is a solution of the Diophantine equation $11x-13y=-17,$ and that $(\overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x,$ what is the value of $\overset{\sim}{x}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, recall that a linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d \: | \: c,$ where $d = \text{gcd}(a,b).$  Moreover, if $(x_0,y_0)$ is a solution to the equation, then the general solution is given by

$$
\left(x_0+\dfrac{b}{d}t, \, y_0-\dfrac{a}{d}t\right), \qquad t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots
$$

Here, we have $a=11,$ $b=-13,$ $c=-17,$ and 

$$
d=\text{gcd}(11,-13)=1.
$$

 

Since $(15,14)$ is a solution of $11x-13y=-17,$ the general solution must be

$$
\left(15+\dfrac{(-13)}{1}t, \, 14-\dfrac{11}{1}t\right) = (15-13t, \, 14-11t),
$$

where $t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \, .$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=15-13t$ is attained when $t=1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{\sim}{x} = 15-13 \cdot 1 = 2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Solving a Linear Diophantine Equation
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the Diophantine equation $2x+7y=10.$ The integer pair $(\overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y})$ is the solution with the smallest possible positive value of $x.$ What is the value of $\overset{\sim}{x}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have the linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

where $a=2,$ $b=7,$ and $c=10.$ We're given that the equation has solutions.

Notice that our equation can't be solved for either of the two variables using integer coefficients. So, let's find the linear representation of $\text{gcd}(2,7)$ using the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}7 & = & 2\cdot 3 & + & 1 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 2 & = & 1\cdot 2 & + & 0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the remainders (the rightmost terms) in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =7-2\cdot 3.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we obtain that $d=\text{gcd}(a,b) = 1$ and

$$
2 \cdot (-3) + 7 = 1.
$$

Multiplying this equation by $10,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot (-3)+7 & =1 \\ 2\cdot (-3)\cdot 10+7\cdot 10 & =10 \\ 2\cdot (-30)+7\cdot 10 & =10,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that $(x,y)=(-30,10)$ is a solution to our Diophantine equation.

Now, the general solution is

$$
\left(-30+\dfrac{b}{d}t, \, 10-\dfrac{a}{d}t\right) = (-30+7t, \, 10-2t),
$$

where $t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \,.$

The smallest possible positive value of $x=-30+7t$ is attained when $t=5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\overset{\sim}{x} = -30+7 \cdot 5 = 5.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **linear Diophantine equation** with two variables $x$ and $y$ takes the form 

$$
ax+by=c,
$$

where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are integer constants. A **solution of a Diophantine equation** is any integer pair 

$$
(x,y)
$$

 that satisfies the equation.

For example, the Diophantine equation 

$$
2x+3y=9
$$

has an infinite number of integer solutions:

$$
(3, 1), \quad (6, -1), \quad (15, -7), \quad \ldots
$$

tutorials.name: When a Linear Diophantine Equation Has No Solutions
tutorials.problem:
The linear Diophantine equation

$$
ax+by=c
$$

has a solution if and only if $d \: | \: c,$ where $d = \text{gcd}(a,b).$  

Let's use the theorem to test some Diophantine equations.

- Consider the equation

$$
2x+10y=17.
$$

Here, we have $a=2,$ $b=10,$ and $c=17.$ Notice that

$$
d=\text{gcd}(2,10)=2
$$

and $2 \!\not{|}\: 17.$ Therefore, according to the theorem, our equation has no solution.

Indeed, notice that the expression on the left-hand side ($2x+10y$) is always an even number, while the right-hand side of the equation ($17$) is an odd number. As a result, there is no solution. 

- Consider the equation

$$
4x+5y=7.
$$

Here, we have $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=7.$ Since 

$$
d=\text{gcd}(4,5)=1
$$

and $1 \:{|}\: 7,$ our equation has solutions.

Indeed, one of the solutions for $4x+5y=7$ is the pair $(3,-1).$

tutorials.name: The General Solution of a Linear Diophantine Equation
tutorials.problem:
If $(x_0,y_0)$ is any particular solution of the equation, then the set of all solutions consists of integer pairs  

$$
\left( x_0 + \dfrac{b}{d}t, \: y_0 - \dfrac{a}{d}t \right), \qquad t = 0, \pm 1, \pm2, \ldots \: .
$$

In particular, if $d=1,$ we obtain

$$
\left( x_0 + bt, \: y_0 - at \right), \qquad t = 0, \pm 1, \pm2, \ldots \: .
$$

For example, given that $(x,y)=(4,-1)$ is a solution of the Diophantine equation 

$$
4x+5y=11,
$$

find its general solution. 

Here, we have $a=4,$ $b=5,$ and $c=11.$ Since $(4,-1)$ is a solution of $4x+5y=11,$ the general solution must be

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\frac{5}{1}t,\,-1-\frac{4}{1}t) & =(4+5t,\,-1-4t),\end{aligned}
$$

where $t=0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots \, .$
